newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African right says it wants talks, not war.
newsitem.headline: S.African right says it wants talks, not war.

text.p: South Africa's right-wing Afrikaners still want a form of self-rule but will negotiate for it rather than go to war, one of their leaders said on Wednesday.

General Constand Viljoen, leader of the Freedom Front, told reporters South Africa's final post-apartheid constitution which took effect earlier this month represented a victory for his party because it made provision for Afrikaner self-determination.

"To start bombing, to start with some degree of applying force, I think at the moment it is wrong," Viljoen said, referring to right-wing radicals who have in recent weeks planted pipe bombs and tried to steal arms from a military base.

"I don't think war is an option at this stage because there is a possibility of a negotiated settlement," said Viljoen, who has acknowledged planning to use force to obtain Afrikaner self-rule before the April 1994 all-race election.
But he added that if South Africa ever appeared to be headed towards communism, he would have to think again about going to war.

Viljoen was chief of the defence force until 1985 and became involved in right-wing politics in the lead-up to the elections, which President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress won with nearly 63 percent of the vote.
The Freedom Front, the only group standing for Afrikaner self-rule that took part in the election, won two percent.

Viljoen said on Wednesday he would have to apply to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for indemnity from prosecution. "I was involved in some resistance measures which can be regarded as sedition," he said.
"Self-determination still is the major drive of the Freedom Front. We are looking for a dispensation in South Africa in which we will have a dignified position as Afrikaner people."
Many of the Afrikaners who once ran South Africa now feel they are being discriminated against by the country's new black rulers.

Mandela's government has set up a committee to research the feasibility of setting aside a territory within South Africa where white Afrikaners, descendants of Dutch, French and German settlers, could exercise a degree of self-rule.
The committee has identified four possible areas -- the arid north-western area of Namaqualand, part of Pretoria, and two other districts in what was once the independent Boer republic of Transvaal.

A member of the committee, Piet Liebenberg, told reporters on Wednesday that to ignore Afrikaner aspirations was to court the kind of ethnic conflict that had torn apart Bosnia, Rwanda and other countries.
"By wishing them away, there is little doubt the frustrations could lead to conflict...(This is) a self- defeating path," he said.
